final_answer: Chromatographic quantification of residual/free BDDE and its hydrolysis products (e.g., HPLC/GC-MS after extraction) against regulatory limits, since unreacted epoxide is the toxic species.
note: Evidence PMC6197218 states quantification of residual BDDE is mandatory and describes detection by combining liquid chromatography and mass spectroscopy (LC-MS), with <2 ppm considered nontoxic.

final_answer: Lyases cleave by beta-elimination, leaving an unsaturated uronate that absorbs at 232 nm (the standard activity readout); vertebrate hyaluronidases hydrolyze the same beta(1->4) bond without the double bond.
note: Evidence PMC6837340 states lyases cleave via beta-elimination producing unsaturated disaccharides while hydrolases add water; PMC11322831 states activity monitored at 232 nm via double bond formation during beta-elimination.

final_answer: LAP absorbs visible light (405 nm) and initiates efficiently at low, cytocompatible doses, whereas Irgacure 2959 needs UV (365 nm) with more phototoxicity risk - LAP is now standard for cell-laden printing.
note: Evidence contains no comparison of LAP vs Irgacure 2959 absorption wavelengths (405 vs 365 nm), initiation efficiency, doses, or phototoxicity; windows are off-topic.

final_answer: Gel fraction (insoluble crosslinked fraction) and equilibrium swelling ratio (water uptake per dry mass), which together report crosslinking efficiency and network density.
note: Evidence only mentions swelling/weight-gain measurement for PVA/HA gels (PMC12564311); no evidence for gel fraction or that these two together are the routine pair for crosslinked HA gel batches.

final_answer: Moist heat depolymerizes HA (large MW and viscosity loss); sterile filtration is also hard for viscous HMW solutions, so aseptic manufacturing or gentler validated methods are used.
note: Evidence does not state moist heat depolymerizes HA or causes MW/viscosity loss, nor filtration difficulty; PMC9495353 instead says autoclaving is frequently used and formulations were sterilized by that method, leaving the draft's rationale unsettled.

final_answer: HA crosslinked with itself: carbodiimide-mediated internal ester bonds between its own carboxyls and hydroxyls, with no foreign crosslinker molecule in the final network.
note: Evidence mentions ACP only as a partially cross-linked granulated HA hydrogel (PMC13006942); no evidence defines ACP as carbodiimide-mediated internal ester bonds with no foreign crosslinker.

final_answer: By competitive binding assays (e.g., ELISA-format competition against labeled native HA) giving IC50 values, or by SPR/BLI with immobilized CD44 - always benchmarked against unmodified HA of matched MW.
note: Evidence PMC4712157 states abilities to inhibit binding of biotinylated HA to CD44 HABD were analyzed using competitive ELISA; PMC11852163 reports binding affinity via KD values from filter binding assay.

final_answer: B - aldehydes, from cleavage of vicinal diols, enabling Schiff-base/hydrazone crosslinking.
note: Evidence PMC11564514 states OHA from periodate (NaIO4) oxidation of HA has numerous aldehyde groups and reacts via Schiff base connections, supporting option B.

final_answer: Hydrogels are loaded differently in different tissues (compression in cartilage, shear in skin/vocal fold); matching the relevant modulus to the target tissue is the design criterion, so both are reported.
note: Evidence reports only shear moduli of vocal fold tissue and HA effects on shear storage modulus/stiffness; no evidence about compressive modulus or tissue-specific loading as the reason both are reported.

final_answer: The precursor is injected as a liquid and gels in place, conforming to irregular defects and avoiding open surgery - at the cost of needing fast, non-toxic gelation chemistry.
note: Evidence PMC4540702 only notes a paste-like system prior to crosslinking for effective delivery in situ; it does not support conforming to irregular defects, avoiding open surgery, or the fast/non-toxic gelation trade-off.

final_answer: Hydrophobic moieties (e.g., 5-beta-cholanic acid or deoxycholic acid) are conjugated to the HA backbone, making an amphiphile that self-assembles in water into nanoparticles with a hydrophobic core and an HA shell.
note: Evidence PMC4425012 states hydrophobic modification drives self-aggregation into nanoparticles with hydrophobic core and hydrophilic shell, and describes coupling hydrophobic DOCA onto HA to form amphiphilic conjugates.

final_answer: The HA shell targets CD44, which is overexpressed on many tumor cells and cancer stem cells, while the core loads hydrophobic drugs; HA is also biocompatible and biodegradable.
note: Evidence PMC3677708 notes drug-resistant tumors and CSC express elevated CD44 binding HA; PMC5223569 states biocompatible biodegradable HA-coated NPs target CD44-overexpressed cells for drug delivery.

final_answer: Rapid hepatic uptake via HARE/Stabilin-2 on liver sinusoidal endothelium (plus hyaluronidase degradation), which competes with tumor accumulation.
note: Evidence PMC7279005 states HA-coated nanoparticles often accumulate in liver due to Stabilin-2 binding and endocytosis; PMC4839745 states HARE/Stab2 in liver sinusoidal endothelial cells are primary scavenger receptors for systemic HA clearance.

final_answer: Binding is multivalent and MW-dependent: longer HA chains generally give stronger avidity for CD44, but also faster clearance; an intermediate MW is usually optimal and must be tuned empirically.
note: Evidence supports multivalent binding (long chains have multiple CD44 sites vs 1-2 for oligomers) but contains nothing on faster clearance of longer chains or an intermediate MW optimum, so the full draft is unsettled.

final_answer: Covalent conjugates such as HA-paclitaxel: the HA backbone targets CD44 and solubilizes the hydrophobic drug, with release by linker cleavage or hyaluronidase at the tumor site.
note: Evidence PMC8391070 describes a paclitaxel polymer conjugate targeting via CD44 receptor-mediated endocytosis and HA-drug conjugate internalization by CD44-overexpressing cells; PMC3677708 covers HA nanogel-drug conjugates improving drug solubility/delivery.

final_answer: Roughly 100-300 nm, with negative zeta potential from the ionized carboxyls of the HA shell.
note: Evidence gives only a single HA-coated formulation example (202.4 nm, -1.90 mV in PMC11376368); it does not establish a typical 100-300 nm range or that negative charge comes from ionized HA carboxyls.

final_answer: Passive accumulation via the EPR effect (leaky tumor vasculature) plus active CD44-mediated binding and endocytosis by tumor cells.
note: Evidence PMC4499038 states nanoparticles are accumulated in tumor tissue by the EPR effect and then target tumor cells by interaction with CD44 followed by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

final_answer: Tumors and endolysosomes are rich in hyaluronidase; enzymatic degradation of the HA shell/backbone at the target site disassembles the carrier and releases the payload locally.
note: Evidence PMC6562767 states HAase acts as a release switch and HA is decomposed by HAase in the cytosol to expose TAT so the particle can release the drug.

final_answer: Surface-coating preformed liposomes with HA by adsorption/conjugation, or anchoring HA-lipid conjugates (e.g., HA-phospholipid) directly in the bilayer - both give a CD44-targeting, negatively charged corona.
note: Evidence supports only HA coating by adsorption onto liposome surface (PMC12524136); no evidence in the pack for the second claimed way, anchoring HA-lipid conjugates directly in the bilayer.

final_answer: Their hydrophobic core can carry imaging payloads - NIR dyes, Raman reporters, or contrast agents - so CD44 targeting concentrates the probe in tumors for fluorescence/photoacoustic/SERS imaging and image-guided surgery.
note: Evidence PMC11340905 states liposome-SERS-HA enabled image-guided tumor surgery; PMC8218930 states HA-based particles serve as contrast agents for NIR-II PA imaging and SERS-based Raman imaging.
